Surge gives a quick start but irregular, stalling growth."],"answer":"Boom (mean 37.5 mm/week, consistent)","figs":["w18-trees"]},{"title":"Comparing two classes","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"The marks of two classes in the same test are: Class A 45, 52, 58, 60, 61, 63, 65, 70, 72, 74; Class B 30, 41, 55, 62, 66, 68, 70, 78, 85, 95. (a) Find the mean, median, range and interquartile range of each class. (b) The standard deviations are 8.5 (A) and 18.5 (B). Compare the classes. (c) Which class would you describe as “better”?"}],"steps":["(a) A: mean $\\tfrac{620}{10}=62$, median $\\tfrac{61+63}{2}=62$, range 29, $Q_1=58$, $Q_3=70$, IQR 12.","B: mean $\\tfrac{650}{10}=65$, median $\\tfrac{66+68}{2}=67$, range 65, $Q_1=55$, $Q_3=78$, IQR 23.","(b) B has a slightly higher average, but its spread (range, IQR, standard deviation) is about twice as large: B has some very strong and some weak students, while A is much more consistent.","(c) It depends on the purpose: B has more high achievers; A has fewer students at risk of failing. A teacher planning extra help would focus on B’s weaker students (Figure 18.2)."],"answer":"(a) A: 62, 62, 29, 12; B: 65, 67, 65, 23 (b) B higher on average, A more consistent","figs":[]},{"title":"The representative average","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A newspaper says “the average rent for a single room in a suburb is GH₵850 a month”. The rents of seven rooms surveyed were GH₵400, 450, 450, 500, 550, 600 and 3000. (a) Find the mean, median and mode. (b) Which average represents the rents best? (c) Is the newspaper’s claim misleading?"}],"steps":["(a) Mean $=\\tfrac{5950}{7}=850$; median $=500$; mode $=450$.","(b) The median (GH₵500): the single rent of GH₵3000 (perhaps a furnished room) pulls the mean far above six of the seven rents.","(c) Yes: GH₵850 is higher than six of the seven rents; “typical” rent is about GH₵500. Seven rooms is also a small sample."],"answer":"(a) 850, 500, 450 (b) the median (c) yes, misleading","figs":[]},{"title":"Screen time and sleep","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"An online health article reports the daily screen time and sleep (hours) of ten teenagers: (3, 7.5), (6, 6.5), (8, 5.2), (5, 6.7), (1, 8.2), (2, 8), (1, 8.5), (6, 6.1), (4, 7), (7, 5.7). (a) Draw a scatter plot and describe the correlation. (b) Use the line $y=8.8-0.44x$ to estimate the sleep of a teenager with 4.5 hours of screen time. (c) Is the study observational or experimental? (d) What can and cannot be concluded?"}],"steps":["(a) Strong negative correlation: more screen time goes with less sleep.","(b) $y\\approx8.8-1.98\\approx6.8$ hours.","(c) Observational: the researchers recorded what teenagers already did.","(d) We can say that screen time and sleep are associated in this sample. We cannot conclude that screens cause less sleep (teenagers who cannot sleep may use screens more), and ten people are too few to represent all teenagers."],"answer":"(a) strong negative (b) about 6.8 h (c) observational (d) association only","figs":["w18-screen"]},{"title":"Goals scored and conceded","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"The goals scored and conceded by seven Ghana Premier League clubs in 2024/25 were: Bibiani 38, 21; Lions 38, 24; Kotoko 37, 27; Nations 40, 21; Dreams 31, 29; Samartex 33, 25; Bechem 32, 28. (a) Present the data in a grouped bar chart and a scatter plot. (b) Describe the correlation between goals scored and goals conceded. (c) Find the mean of each. (d) What might explain the trend, and what are the limitations?"}],"steps":["(a) Bar chart: two bars per club; scatter: goals scored on the $x$-axis, conceded on the $y$-axis.","(b) Negative correlation: clubs that score more tend to concede fewer.","(c) Mean scored $\\tfrac{249}{7}\\approx35.6$; mean conceded $\\tfrac{175}{7}=25$.","(d) Stronger clubs dominate possession, so they both attack more and defend less often. Limitations: only seven clubs and one season; Kotoko (37 scored, 27 conceded) does not fit the pattern well."],"answer":"(b) negative (c) 35.6 and 25","figs":["w18-football","w18-goals"]},{"title":"A truncated axis","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"An advert shows a bar chart in which Brand Y’s bar looks three times as tall as Brand X’s. The labels show sales of 98 000 (X) and 102 000 (Y) units, and the vertical axis starts at 96 000. (a) Explain why the chart misleads. (b) Find the true percentage difference. (c) Describe an honest chart."}],"steps":["(a) Starting the axis at 96 000 shows only the top of each bar: X’s bar is 2 units tall and Y’s is 6, so Y looks three times as large.","(b) $\\dfrac{102\\,000-98\\,000}{98\\,000}\\times100\\%\\approx4.1\\%$.","(c) Start the axis at 0 (or mark a clear break) and label it; the bars will then be almost equal (Figure 18.3)."],"answer":"(b) about 4.1% more","figs":[]},{"title":"Counts or rates?","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A radio report says Region A had 500 cases of a disease and Region B only 300, “so Region A is the worse affected”. The populations are 2.5 million and 0.8 million. (a) Calculate the rate per 100 000 people for each region. (b) Is the report’s conclusion correct?"}],"steps":["(a) A: $\\dfrac{500}{2\\,500\\,000}\\times100\\,000=20$ per 100 000. B: $\\dfrac{300}{800\\,000}\\times100\\,000=37.5$ per 100 000.","(b) No. Region B has almost twice the rate of Region A; A simply has more people."],"answer":"(a) 20 and 37.5 per 100 000 (b) no: B is worse affected","figs":[]},{"title":"Percentage changes in the news","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"The price of a bag of cement rose from GH₵80 to GH₵100, and later the newspaper reported “a 25% fall” from GH₵100. (a) Find the percentage rise. (b) Find the price after the 25% fall. (c) A reader says the price is now back to GH₵80. Explain the error."}],"steps":["(a) $\\dfrac{100-80}{80}\\times100\\%=25\\%$.","(b) $100\\times0.75=75$, that is GH₵75.","(c) Percentages are taken of different starting values: 25% of 80 is 20, but 25% of 100 is 25. To return to GH₵80 the price would need to fall by $\\tfrac{20}{100}=20\\%$."],"answer":"(a) 25% (b) GH₵75 (c) the base changes","figs":[]},{"title":"Judging a media claim","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A social-media post says: “4 out of 5 doctors recommend Brand Z toothpaste.” (a) List four questions you should ask before believing it. (b) What would make the claim more trustworthy?"}],"steps":["(a) How many doctors were asked (5, or 500)? How were they chosen, and who paid for the survey? What exactly was the question (recommend Brand Z only, or among several brands)? Who published it, and is the source named?","(b) A named, independent source; a large random sample of dentists and doctors; the full question and all the results, including how many recommended other brands."],"answer":"Ask about the sample size, selection, question, sponsor and source.","figs":[]},{"title":"Using data in a debate","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"For a debate on “The rise of HIV/AIDS cases in Ghana: a cause for worry or a mere public scare”, a speaker quotes these figures from the Teacher Manual: about 334 721 people living with HIV in 2024; adult prevalence 1.7%; 17 774 new infections in 2023 (1698 of them children); about 50 new infections a day; 12 614 AIDS-related deaths in 2023. (a) Check that “about 50 a day” agrees with the yearly figure. (b) What percentage of new infections were children? (c) Prevalence has stayed near 1.6–1.7% while the number of people living with HIV has grown. Give two possible reasons. (d) Some of the figures are credited to social-media pages. How should the speaker improve the evidence?"}],"steps":["(a) $17\\,774\\div365\\approx48.7$, about 50 a day ✓.","(b) $\\dfrac{1698}{17\\,774}\\times100\\%\\approx9.6\\%$.","(c) The population is growing, so the same percentage is a larger number; and treatment (antiretroviral therapy) helps people with HIV live longer, so more people are living with HIV even if infection rates are steady. A rising **number** does not by itself mean a rising **rate**.","(d) Use the Ghana AIDS Commission, Ghana Health Service, UNAIDS or WHO directly, give the year of each figure, compare rates over several years, and present them in a clear chart."],"answer":"(a) 48.7 ≈ 50 a day (b) about 9.6% (c) population growth; longer survival on treatment","figs":[]}],"summary":[{"title":"Key results","items":["Bivariate comparisons: direction, strength, gradient, level and consistency; strength ≠ gradient.","Univariate comparisons: mean, median, mode; range, IQR, standard deviation; box plots.","Use the median for skewed data with outliers.","Compare regions by rates per 100 000, not counts.","Percentage change $=\\dfrac{\\text{new}-\\text{old}}{\\text{old}}\\times100\\%$; successive percentages use different bases.","Check sources, samples, axes and claims of cause before trusting media data."]}],"quiz":[{"q":"Two scatter graphs both show points lying very close to straight lines, one steep and one gentle. Both show","options":["strong correlation","weak correlation","no correlation","negative correlation"],"correct":0,"explain":"Strength is closeness to a line, not steepness."},{"q":"Which average is least affected by one very large value?","options":["the median","the mean","the total","the range"],"correct":0,"explain":"It depends only on the middle value."},{"q":"Data set P has IQR 6 and data set Q has IQR 15. Which is more consistent?","options":["P","Q","they are equally consistent","it cannot be decided"],"correct":0,"explain":"The smaller spread."},{"q":"A town of 400 000 people records 60 cases. The percentage increase is","options":["25%","20%","10%","50%"],"correct":0,"explain":"$\\tfrac{10}{40}$."},{"q":"A bar chart’s vertical axis starts at 90 instead of 0. This","options":["exaggerates differences between bars","makes the chart more accurate","has no effect","hides the largest bar"],"correct":0,"explain":"A truncated axis."},{"q":"“3 out of 4 customers prefer our bread” is weak evidence if","options":["only four customers were asked","the bread is cheap","the data are in a table","it is printed in a newspaper"],"correct":0,"explain":"The sample may be tiny."},{"q":"The most reliable source for Ghana’s population figures is","options":["the Ghana Statistical Service","an anonymous WhatsApp message","a radio phone-in caller","an advertisement"],"correct":0,"explain":"The official statistics office."},{"q":"The median of 3, 9, 4, 12, 7, 5 is","options":["6","7","5","6.67"],"correct":0,"explain":"Ordered: 3, 4, 5, 7, 9, 12; $\\tfrac{5+7}{2}$."},{"q":"A value of 120 increased by 10% and then decreased by 10% gives","options":["118.8","120","121.2","108"],"correct":0,"explain":"$120\\times1.1\\times0.9$."}],"exercise":[{"q":"Two machines’ outputs over six days: A 50, 52, 49, 51, 50, 48; B 40, 62, 55, 45, 60, 38. (c) A supplier wants a reliable customer who orders about the same number every day. Whom should she choose? Justify your answer.","steps":[],"answer":"","model":[{"k":"p","text":"(a) Ama: sum 240, mean 24, ordered 22, 22, 22, 23, 24, 24, 25, 25, 26, 27, median 24, range 5. Kwesi: sum 250, mean 25, ordered 15, 16, 18, 20, 22, 28, 30, 32, 34, 35, median 25, range 20."},{"k":"p","text":"(b) Ama’s daily sales vary little about her mean; Kwesi’s vary about four times as much."},{"k":"p","text":"(c) Ama: although her mean is slightly lower, her sales are far more predictable, so her orders will be steady."}]},{"q":"A newspaper reports: “Crime in City X has doubled! 200 cases in March compared with 100 in February.” (a) Give three reasons why this conclusion may be misleading. It means that in conditions like these, rain fell on about 70 days out of 100.","**A 70% chance of winning is not a guarantee.** In 10 such matches the team is expected to win about 7 and lose or draw about 3.","**“87% effective”** means the vaccinated group’s risk is 87% lower than the unvaccinated group’s, not that 87 of every 100 doses work.","**The gambler’s fallacy:** past results do not change the probability of independent events. (a) What does this mean? (b) In 20 matches with the same 70% chance, how many wins are expected? (c) Medeama loses. Was the prediction “wrong”? (d) How might fans and bettors react?"}],"steps":["(a) In many matches like this one, Medeama would be expected to win about 70 out of 100; a win is likely but not certain.","(b) $20\\times0.7=14$ wins.","(c) Not necessarily: a 30% event happens about 3 times in 10. A forecast is judged over many predictions, not one.","(d) Fans may feel confident; some bettors back Medeama, others back the opponent hoping for an upset at bigger odds."],"answer":"(b) 14 (c) not necessarily","figs":[]},{"title":"Relative and absolute risk","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A headline says: “Eating food fried in reused oil doubles your risk of a rare stomach illness!” The risk rises from 1 in 10 000 to 2 in 10 000 people per year. (a) Find the relative and absolute increase. (b) Is the headline false? Is it misleading? (c) What should a careful reader do?"}],"steps":["(a) Relative increase $=\\dfrac{2-1}{1}\\times100\\%=100\\%$ (“doubles”). Absolute increase $=\\dfrac{1}{10\\,000}=0.01$ percentage points.","(b) Not false, but misleading: for 10 000 people, only one extra case a year.","(c) Ask for the absolute risks, the size of the study, who funded it, and whether the effect is causal; then weigh it against other risks."],"answer":"(a) 100% relative, 0.01 percentage points absolute","figs":[]},{"title":"Reading betting odds","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A bookmaker offers decimal odds for Hearts of Oak against Asante Kotoko: Hearts win 2.10, draw 3.20, Kotoko win 3.50. (a) Find the implied probabilities and their total. (b) Explain the total. (c) Scaling the implied probabilities so they add to 1 gives a fair probability of a Hearts win of about 0.443. Find the expected gain on a GH₵10 bet on Hearts."}],"steps":["(a) $\\dfrac{1}{2.10}\\approx0.476$, $\\dfrac{1}{3.20}\\approx0.313$, $\\dfrac{1}{3.50}\\approx0.286$; total $\\approx1.074$.","(b) The extra 0.074 (7.4%) is the bookmaker’s margin: the odds are set below fair values so that the bookmaker profits over many bets.","(c) Win: return GH₵21 (gain GH₵11) with probability 0.443; lose GH₵10 with probability 0.557.","Expected gain $=0.443\\times11-0.557\\times10=4.87-5.57\\approx-0.70$: on average the bettor loses about 70 pesewas per GH₵10."],"answer":"(a) 0.476, 0.313, 0.286; total 1.074 (c) about −GH₵0.70","figs":[]},{"title":"Is the raffle worth it?","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A school sells 2000 raffle tickets at GH₵5 each. The prizes are one of GH₵2000, four of GH₵500 and twenty of GH₵50. (a) Find the probability that a ticket wins a prize. (b) Find the expected value of the prizes per ticket. (c) Find the expected gain of buying one ticket. (d) Why is the raffle still acceptable as a fund-raiser?"}],"steps":["(a) $\\dfrac{1+4+20}{2000}=\\dfrac{25}{2000}=0.0125$.","(b) Total prizes $=2000+2000+1000=5000$; per ticket $\\dfrac{5000}{2000}=2.50$, that is GH₵2.50.","(c) $2.50-5=-2.50$: an expected loss of GH₵2.50 per ticket.","(d) Buyers knowingly donate to the school; the expected loss is the donation, and the school raises GH₵10 000 − GH₵5000 = GH₵5000."],"answer":"(a) 0.0125 (b) GH₵2.50 (c) −GH₵2.50","figs":[]},{"title":"Setting an insurance premium","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"An insurer estimates that the probability of a particular motorbike being stolen in a year is 0.02. The motorbike is worth GH₵15 000. (a) Find the expected yearly payout per motorbike. (b) The insurer charges GH₵450 a year. How much of this covers expected claims, and what is the rest for? (c) Why does insurance make sense for the owner even though the expected value is negative?"}],"steps":["(a) $0.02\\times15\\,000=300$, that is GH₵300.","(b) GH₵300 covers expected claims; GH₵150 covers administration, staff and profit.","(c) A loss of GH₵15 000 would be a disaster for the owner, while GH₵450 is affordable. Insurance spreads the cost of rare large losses over many people."],"answer":"(a) GH₵300 (b) GH₵150 for costs and profit","figs":[]},{"title":"Lending and default risk","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A microfinance company estimates a 30% chance that a new borrower will not repay. It lends GH₵1000 each to 200 new borrowers. (a) How many defaults are expected? (b) If defaulters repay nothing, what must each repaying borrower pay back for the company to recover all GH₵200 000? (c) What interest rate is this? (d) Comment on fairness."}],"steps":["(a) $200\\times0.3=60$ defaults, so 140 repay.","(b) $\\dfrac{200\\,000}{140}\\approx1428.57$, that is about GH₵1428.57 each.","(c) About 42.9% interest just to break even, before any costs or profit.","(d) Honest borrowers pay for defaulters; better checks on borrowers (lowering the default probability) would allow lower interest rates."],"answer":"(a) 60 (b) about GH₵1428.57 (c) about 42.9%","figs":[]},{"title":"An opinion poll","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A poll of 1000 voters in a region gives Candidate A 52% and Candidate B 48%, with a margin of error of ±3 percentage points. A radio presenter says “Candidate A will win.” (a) Find the likely range of support for each. (b) Is the presenter’s statement justified? (c) How might such a statement affect voters?"}],"steps":["(a) A: 49% to 55%; B: 45% to 51%.","(b) No. The ranges overlap, so B could actually be ahead; the race is too close to call.","(c) Supporters of A may stay at home thinking the result is decided, while B’s supporters may work harder: polls can change behaviour."],"answer":"(a) 49–55% and 45–51% (b) no: too close to call","figs":[]},{"title":"The gambler’s fallacy","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"(a) A coin has shown heads five times in a row. Kofi says tails is “due”. Is he right? (b) A teacher says “Probability has come up in the last three papers, so it is unlikely this year.” Comment. (c) A lottery player always avoids last week’s numbers. Does this change her chance of winning?"}],"steps":["(a) No. Coin tosses are independent: $P(\\text{tails})=\\tfrac12$ on the next toss whatever happened before.","(b) Unless examiners deliberately rotate topics, past papers do not make a topic less likely; core topics such as probability often appear every year. Skipping it is a high-risk strategy.","(c) No. Every set of numbers has the same chance in each draw."],"answer":"(a) no (b) not a safe inference (c) no","figs":[]},{"title":"Probabilities from weather data","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"The illustrative monthly data show rainfall (mm) and mean temperature (°C) for a town in southern Ghana. Temperature is “high” if $t\\ge28.8$°C and rainfall is “heavy” if $f\\ge100$ mm. Taking each month as equally likely: (a) find P(low temperature) (b) find P(heavy rainfall) (c) find P(low temperature and heavy rainfall) (d) find P(low temperature, given heavy rainfall) (e) explain (c) to a layperson."}],"steps":["(a) Low temperatures in June, July, August, September and October: $P=\\dfrac{5}{12}$.","(b) Heavy rain in April, May, June, September and October: $P=\\dfrac{5}{12}$.","(c) Both in June, September and October: $P=\\dfrac{3}{12}=\\dfrac14$.","(d) Of the 5 heavy-rain months, 3 are cool: $\\dfrac35$.","(e) “In about one month out of every four, it is both cooler than usual and very rainy, so plan for both together then.” Note the data are monthly averages for one location and may differ from year to year."],"answer":"(a) $\\tfrac{5}{12}$ (b) $\\tfrac{5}{12}$ (c) $\\tfrac14$ (d) $\\tfrac35$","figs":["w19-weather"]},{"title":"Bed nets and malaria","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A district report says: “Of 1500 children who did not sleep under treated nets, 120 had malaria last year; of 1000 who did, 40 had malaria.” (a) Find the experimental probability of malaria in each group. (b) Find the absolute and relative reduction. (c) A newspaper writes “Nets halve malaria.” Is this justified? What else would you want to know?"}],"steps":["(a) Without nets: $\\dfrac{120}{1500}=0.08$ (8%). With nets: $\\dfrac{40}{1000}=0.04$ (4%).","(b) Absolute reduction 4 percentage points; relative reduction $\\dfrac{8-4}{8}=50\\%$.","(c) “Halves” matches these figures, but this is observational: families who use nets may also live in better housing or nearer clinics. Ask how children were chosen, whether other factors were similar, and whether the result is repeated in other districts. Controlled trials elsewhere support the benefit of treated nets."],"answer":"(a) 0.08 and 0.04 (b) 4 points; 50%","figs":[]}],"summary":[{"title":"Key results","items":["$0\\le P(A)\\le1$; $P(\\text{not }A)=1-P(A)$; expected count $=nP(A)$.","Experimental probability $=\\dfrac{\\text{frequency}}{\\text{trials}}$, approaching the true value for many trials.","Relative change $=\\dfrac{p_2-p_1}{p_1}$; absolute change $=p_2-p_1$.","Implied probability $=\\dfrac{1}{\\text{odds}}$; totals above 1 show the bookmaker’s margin.","Expected value $E=\\sum x\\,P(x)$; a fair game has expected gain 0.","Independent events have no memory (gambler’s fallacy)."]}],"quiz":[{"q":"A forecast of “30% chance of rain” means","options":["on days like this, rain falls about 3 times in 10","it will rain for 30% of the day","30% of the region will get rain","it will definitely not rain"],"correct":0,"explain":"It is a relative frequency."},{"q":"A team has a 0.6 probability of winning each match. In 15 such matches the expected number of wins is","options":["9","6","10","15"],"correct":0,"explain":"$15\\times0.6$."},{"q":"Decimal odds of 4.00 imply a probability of","options":["0.25","0.4","4","0.75"],"correct":0,"explain":"$\\tfrac14$."},{"q":"A risk rises from 2% to 3%. The relative increase is","options":["50%","1%","33%","150%"],"correct":0,"explain":"$\\tfrac{1}{2}$."},{"q":"A raffle ticket costs GH₵2 and the expected prize per ticket is GH₵0.80. The expected gain is","options":["−GH₵1.20","GH₵0.80","GH₵1.20","−GH₵0.80"],"correct":0,"explain":"$0.80-2$."},{"q":"After four tails in a row with a fair coin, the probability of heads on the next toss is","options":["$\\tfrac12$","more than $\\tfrac12$","less than $\\tfrac12$","1"],"correct":0,"explain":"Tosses are independent."},{"q":"A vaccine is 80% effective and the unvaccinated risk is 10%. The vaccinated risk is","options":["2%","8%","80%","10%"],"correct":0,"explain":"$10\\%\\times0.2$."},{"q":"A poll gives 54% ± 4%. The likely range is","options":["50% to 58%","54% to 58%","46% to 54%","52% to 56%"],"correct":0,"explain":"$54\\pm4$."},{"q":"A coin tossed 500 times shows 262 heads. The experimental probability of heads is","options":["0.524","0.5","0.262","0.476"],"correct":0,"explain":"$\\tfrac{262}{500}$."},{"q":"The implied probabilities from a bookmaker’s odds add up to 1.08. This shows","options":["the bookmaker’s margin","a mistake by the bookmaker","a fair game","that every bettor wins"],"correct":0,"explain":"The extra 8% favours the bookmaker."}],"exercise":[{"q":"A forecast gives an 85% chance of rain. Find the probability of no rain and say what a farmer drying cocoa beans should do.","a":"0.15; cover or move the beans"},{"q":"A team’s chance of winning each match is 0.45. How many wins are expected in a 30-match season?","a":"13.5, about 13 or 14"},{"q":"Convert decimal odds of 1.60, 2.50 and 5.00 into implied probabilities.","a":"0.625, 0.4, 0.2"},{"q":"The odds for a two-way contest are 1.80 and 2.05. Find the bookmaker’s margin.","a":"$0.556+0.488=1.044$: 4.4%"},{"q":"A risk falls from 12% to 9%. Find the absolute and relative reductions.","a":"3 points; 25%"},{"q":"A lottery sells 50 000 tickets at GH₵2 and pays prizes totalling GH₵40 000. Find the expected loss per ticket.","a":"$2-0.80=$ GH₵1.20"},{"q":"An insurer pays GH₵8000 if a shop burns down, with probability 0.005 a year. Find the expected payout and suggest a fair premium.","a":"GH₵40; a premium above GH₵40, e.g. GH₵60"},{"q":"A die is rolled 600 times and shows 6 on 130 rolls. Is the die likely to be fair?","a":"Expected 100; 130 is quite high: test further"},{"q":"A newspaper says “Using phones while driving makes you four times as likely to crash.” What extra information is needed?","a":"The baseline risk, the study size and design"},{"q":"Of 800 patients, 56 had side effects from a drug. Estimate the probability of side effects and the number expected in 5000 patients.","a":"0.07; 350"},{"q":"A poll shows 47% for and 45% against with ±3%. Can the presenter say “a majority is for”?","a":"No: ranges overlap and 47% is not over 50%"},{"q":"Explain why a gambler who has lost ten times in a row should not expect to win next.","a":"Independent events: the chance is unchanged"}],"theory":[{"q":"Individual research. Choose three probability statements from named Ghanaian or international media (for example GMet, Joy FM, TV3, Daily Graphic, a health website), with the date you saw them. For each: (a) write the statement and source (b) explain its meaning simply (c) give two common misconceptions (d) give three real-life effects on decisions. Then answer: (e) Why should the media explain probabilities clearly? (f) How can schools reduce misunderstanding?","steps":[],"answer":"","model":[{"k":"p","text":"A good answer gives full statements with source and date, for example “There is an 80% chance of rain in Accra tomorrow” (GMet, accessed on a stated date); a plain explanation (“on 80 of 100 similar days, it rained”); misconceptions (rain for 80% of the day; rain is certain); effects (carry umbrellas, postpone outdoor events, farmers delay spraying)."},{"k":"p","text":"(e) Because people act on these numbers; unclear statements lead to poor decisions, panic or complacency."},{"k":"p","text":"(f) Teach probability through real forecasts, health and sport examples; practise converting between percentages, fractions, odds and expected numbers; and discuss absolute versus relative risk."}]},{"q":"A health campaign says a new malaria vaccine is 75% effective. In a district, the yearly risk of malaria for an unvaccinated child is 20%, and there are 12 000 children. (a) Find the expected number of cases without vaccination. (b) Find the expected number if 60% of the children are vaccinated. (c) Find the absolute and relative risk for a vaccinated child. (d) Write a short paragraph for a radio announcement that explains the vaccine’s benefit honestly.","steps":[],"answer":"","model":[{"k":"p","text":"(a) $12\\,000\\times0.2=2400$ cases."},{"k":"p","text":"(b) Vaccinated: $7200$ children, risk $20\\%\\times0.25=5\\%$, so $360$ cases. Unvaccinated: $4800\\times0.2=960$. Total $1320$: about 1080 cases prevented."},{"k":"p","text":"(c) Absolute risk 5% (down from 20%, a fall of 15 points); relative reduction 75%."},{"k":"p","text":"(d) “In our district about 1 child in 5 gets malaria each year. With the vaccine this falls to about 1 child in 20. It does not give complete protection, so keep sleeping under treated nets, but vaccinating most children could prevent around a thousand cases a year.”"}]},{"q":"A betting company offers the following odds for a match: Team P win 1.70, draw 3.60, Team Q win 5.50. (a) Find the implied probabilities and the margin. (b) Adjust the implied probabilities so that they add to 1. (c) Find the expected gain on a GH₵20 bet on Team Q. (d) Explain, using expected value, why betting is not a way to make money in the long run, and give one social effect of heavy betting among young people.","steps":[],"answer":"","model":[{"k":"p","text":"(a) $\\tfrac{1}{1.70}\\approx0.588$, $\\tfrac{1}{3.60}\\approx0.278$, $\\tfrac{1}{5.50}\\approx0.182$; total $\\approx1.048$, a margin of about 4.8%."},{"k":"p","text":"(b) Divide each by 1.048: about 0.561, 0.265 and 0.174."},{"k":"p","text":"(c) Win: gain $20\\times4.5=90$ with probability 0.174; lose 20 with probability 0.826. Expected gain $\\approx15.66-16.52=-0.86$, a loss of about GH₵0.86."},{"k":"p","text":"(d) Because the odds include the bookmaker’s margin, every bet has a negative expected value: over many bets the bettor loses about the margin on each cedi staked. Socially, heavy betting can lead to debt, loss of school fees and savings, and addiction."}]},{"q":"The table shows the number of floods recorded in a district over 40 years, by month of the rainy season: April 2, May 6, June 14, July 5, September 3, October 8, other months 2. (a) Find the probability that a flood in this district occurs in June. (b) Find the experimental probability that a given year has a flood in June, if June floods occurred in 14 of the 40 years. (c) How should NADMO use this information? (d) State two limitations of using past data to predict floods.","steps":[],"answer":"","model":[{"k":"p","text":"(a) Total floods $=2+6+14+5+3+8+2=40$; $P(\\text{June}\\mid\\text{flood})=\\tfrac{14}{40}=0.35$."},{"k":"p","text":"(b) $\\tfrac{14}{40}=0.35$ per year."},{"k":"p","text":"(c) Pre-position boats, food and medicine and clear drains before June and October, and run evacuation drills in the most flood-prone areas."},{"k":"p","text":"(d) Climate change and new building on flood plains may make the past a poor guide; 40 years is a limited record, and recording methods may have changed."}]},{"q":"(a) Explain the difference between theoretical and experimental probability, with an example of each. (b) Describe a class experiment to estimate the probability that a bottle top lands face up, and explain how you would make the estimate reliable. (c) If the class finds 172 face-up results in 400 throws, estimate the probability and the expected number of face-up results in 1500 throws.","steps":[],"answer":"","model":[{"k":"p","text":"(a) Theoretical probability uses equally likely outcomes, for example $P(\\text{six})=\\tfrac16$ for a fair die. Experimental probability uses observed frequencies, for example 43 rainy days out of 120 gives $\\tfrac{43}{120}$."},{"k":"p","text":"(b) Each student throws the same kind of bottle top from the same height onto the same surface 20 times, recording the results; combine the class results. Many throws make the relative frequency stable."},{"k":"p","text":"(c) $\\tfrac{172}{400}=0.43$; expected in 1500 throws $=1500\\times0.43=645$."}]}],"checklist":["I can name uses of probability in Ghanaian media and institutions.","I can interpret forecasts, effectiveness figures and predictions correctly.","I can find experimental probabilities and expected numbers.","I can convert odds to probabilities and find a bookmaker’s margin.","I can distinguish relative from absolute risk.","I can use expected value to judge raffles, bets and insurance.","I can explain the gambler’s fallacy and other misconceptions."],"plan":{"lessons":[[{"j":0,"notes":true,"exs":[]},{"j":1,"notes":true,"exs":[]},{"j":2,"notes":true,"exs":[0,1,2,3,4]}],[{"j":2,"notes":false,"exs":[5,6,7,8,9,10,11]},{"j":3,"notes":true,"exs":[]}]],"exSec":[2,2,2,2,2,2,2,2,2,2,2,2],"quizSec":[2,2,3,2,3,2,2,0,0,3],"exerSec":[2,2,3,3,2,3,0,3,0,1,1,2],"thSec":[2,2,3,0,0],"sumSec":[3,0,2,3,3,2],"chkSec":[1,2,3,3,2,3,2],"weights":[1101.3,596.25,9694,1268.7],"figs":[{"id":"w19-scale","sec":0,"lesson":1,"caption":"From impossible to certain."},{"id":"w19-odds","sec":3,"lesson":2,"caption":"Implied probabilities add up to more than 1."}]},"next":"Probability II: Dependent and Independent Events","tm":{"sectionNo":5,"sectionName":"Data Handling and Probability","strand":"Making Sense of and Using Data","sub":"Probability/Chance","cs":["Demonstrate conceptual understanding of probability involving two dependent and independent events, and use it to make decisions in real-life situations."],"lo":["Explain how a given probability from print and electronic media influences individual decisions;
